# Py Lab 5 {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Data visualization I {.smaller}

The lecture established that adult asthma prevalence barely varies across Pennsylvania
counties — 9.7% to 11.6% — while smoking prevalence varies across eleven points, and that the
two move together at **+0.659**.

This lab builds seven figures from four real files with matplotlib and seaborn, then repairs
one figure that runs without error and misleads anyway.

::: {.callout-note}
## Lab mechanics
- Each exercise supplies a worked example, then a similar problem to complete.
- Click into a code block and press **Run**. Edit the blanks (`____`) and run again.
- **Hint** gives the reasoning. **Solution** gives the answer.
- Each exercise takes two slides: the worked example, then the task.
- Arrow keys navigate between slides.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## One of these exercises contains no error message
Exercise 8 supplies a figure that executes cleanly and states something false. A figure that
raises no exception has not been checked — it has only been run.
:::

## The data {.smaller}

Four real files, all mounted and readable with `pd.read_csv()`.

| File | Rows | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv` | 67 | Asthma, **smoking**, obesity prevalence — CDC PLACES 2024 |
| `data/pa_counties.csv` | 67 | Population, **region**, **metro/nonmetro** — the join target |
| `data/pa_maternal_infant.csv` | 67 | Infant mortality, poverty, income — 23 counties suppressed |
| `data/pa_covid_monthly.csv` | 3,283 | COVID deaths by county and month — reliable from mid-2021 |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Three facts that recur throughout
**A rate is** `deaths / population * 100000`. **A blank is suppression**, not zero. Neither
`region` nor `metro` appears in any outcome file, so every grouped figure below requires a
join first.
:::

## The course figure palette {.smaller}

Every colour below was measured against white with the WCAG relative luminance formula. A
mark that carries data needs **3:1**; text needs **4.5:1**.

| Colour | Ratio | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `#003594` royal | **10.84 : 1** | The primary series |
| `#8a6400` dark gold | **5.38 : 1** | The second series |
| `#6b7280` gray | **4.83 : 1** | Annotation and source notes |

::: {.callout-warning}
## No two of these separate from each other by 3:1
Royal against dark gold is **2.02:1**. Each is readable against the page; they are not
reliably distinguishable from one another. **Every two-series figure in this lab therefore
carries a second channel** — a marker shape, a dash pattern, or a direct label.
:::

# Exercise 1 — A histogram shows a distribution {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 1 — A histogram shows a distribution {.smaller}

**Worked example.** A histogram bins a continuous variable and counts what lands in each bin.
`ax.axvline()` adds a reference line, identified in the title so colour is not the only cue.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of adult smoking prevalence across 67 counties with a dashed vertical line marking the state mean of 17.1 percent."
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
state_mean = asthma["smoking_prev_pct"].mean()             # the value the line marks

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.hist(asthma["smoking_prev_pct"], bins=12,               # layer 1: the histogram
        color="#003594", edgecolor="white")                # fill; white gaps between bars
ax.axvline(state_mean, color="#8a6400",                    # layer 2: a vertical line at the mean
           linestyle="--", linewidth=2)                    # dashed, thicker than default
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")              # x-axis label with units
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")                        # y-axis label
ax.set_title(f"Smoking prevalence (dashed line = mean, {state_mean:.1f}%)")  # names the line
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 1.** Histogram of adult smoking prevalence across 67 counties with a dashed vertical line marking the state mean of 17.1 percent.
:::

## Exercise 1 — A histogram shows a distribution — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw the distribution of **infant mortality** across the counties that publish a
rate, and mark the **median** with a dashed line. Use `infant_mortality_per_1000` from `data/pa_maternal_infant.csv`. `reporting` keeps the rows where it is present; `state_median` is their median.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex1_histogram
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")        # one row per county
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])  # drop suppressed counties

state_median = reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"].____()     # the value the line marks

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.hist(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"], bins=10,   # layer 1: the histogram
        color="#003594", edgecolor="white")                # fill; white gaps between bars
ax.axvline(state_median, color="#8a6400",                  # layer 2: a line at the median
           linestyle="--", linewidth=2)                    # dashed, thicker than default
ax.set_xlabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")       # x-axis label with units
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")                        # y-axis label
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality, 44 reporting counties (dashed = median, {state_median:.1f})")  # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

print("counties plotted:", len(reporting))                 # how many counties are drawn
print("median:", round(state_median, 2))                   # the marked value
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex1_histogram
#| hint: true
# The blank is median.
#
# .dropna(subset=[...]) removes only the rows missing that column, so 44
# counties survive — the 23 suppressed ones are gone. Say so in the title,
# as the code already does. A figure that silently drops a third of the
# state is the kind of figure this course is trying not to produce.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex1_histogram
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")        # one row per county
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])  # drop suppressed counties

state_median = reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"].median()   # the value the line marks

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.hist(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"], bins=10,   # layer 1: the histogram
        color="#003594", edgecolor="white")                # fill; white gaps between bars
ax.axvline(state_median, color="#8a6400",                  # layer 2: a line at the median
           linestyle="--", linewidth=2)                    # dashed, thicker than default
ax.set_xlabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")       # x-axis label with units
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")                        # y-axis label
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality, 44 reporting counties (dashed = median, {state_median:.1f})")  # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

print("counties plotted:", len(reporting))                 # how many counties are drawn
print("median:", round(state_median, 2))                   # the marked value
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex1_histogram
#| check: true
assert len(reporting) == 44, "44 counties publish an infant mortality rate."          # suppression handled
assert abs(state_median - 6.0) < 0.001, "The median is 6.0 per 1,000."                 # the right statistic
assert len(ax.lines) >= 1, "Draw the median as a vertical line."                       # the reference layer
assert ax.get_xlabel() != "" and ax.get_ylabel() != "", "Label both axes."             # labels present
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The 44 belongs in the title
Twenty-three counties are absent from this figure, and they are disproportionately rural.
A reader who is not told that will read it as a picture of Pennsylvania.
:::

# Exercise 2 — Bars compare categories {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 2 — Bars compare categories {.smaller}

**Worked example.** `ax.bar()` compares one value across named categories; `ax.barh()` draws
the bars sideways. Sorting before plotting delivers the ranking to the reader for free.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of the five Pennsylvania counties with the highest adult smoking prevalence, ranging from about 20.7 to 21.8 percent."
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
top5 = (asthma.nlargest(5, "smoking_prev_pct")             # the five highest rows ...
              .sort_values("smoking_prev_pct"))            # ... in ascending order

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.barh(top5["county"], top5["smoking_prev_pct"],          # one horizontal bar per county
        color="#003594")                                   # fill colour
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")              # x-axis label with units
ax.set_title("Five highest county smoking rates")          # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 2.** Horizontal bar chart of the five Pennsylvania counties with the highest adult smoking prevalence, ranging from about 20.7 to 21.8 percent.
:::

## Exercise 2 — Bars compare categories — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw the five counties with the **lowest** smoking prevalence. Use
`.nsmallest()`, and sort so the bars run in order. Use `smoking_prev_pct` from `data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv`, sort `bottom5` lowest first, and draw horizontal bars with `ax.barh()`.

```{pyodide}

import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
bottom5 = (asthma.____(5, "smoking_prev_pct")              # the five lowest rows ...
                 .sort_values("smoking_prev_pct"))         # ... lowest first

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.barh(bottom5["county"], bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"],    # one horizontal bar per county
        color="#003594")                                   # fill colour
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")              # x-axis label with units
ax.set_title("Five lowest county smoking rates")           # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

print(bottom5[["county", "smoking_prev_pct"]].to_string(index=False))  # the five, as a table
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars
#| hint: true
# The blank is nsmallest.
#
# .nlargest(n, col) and .nsmallest(n, col) both return whole rows, not
# just the column — which is why `bottom5["county"]` still works.
# Chester should come out at the bottom, at 10.6%.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars

ax.barh(bottom5["county"], bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"],    # one horizontal bar per county
        color="#003594")                                   # fill colour

```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex2_bars
#| check: true
assert len(bottom5) == 5, "Five counties."                                             # five rows
assert bottom5["county"].iloc[0] == "Chester", "Chester has the lowest smoking prevalence, 10.6%."  # right end
assert abs(bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"].min() - 10.6) < 0.001, "The minimum is 10.6%."  # right value
assert bottom5["smoking_prev_pct"].is_monotonic_increasing, "Sort before plotting."    # sorted
assert len(ax.patches) == 5, "Five bars must be drawn."                                # five bars
```

# Exercise 3 — A boxplot compares groups {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 3 — A boxplot compares groups {.smaller}

**Worked example.** A boxplot marks the **median** (the line), the **interquartile range** (the
box), and the spread beyond it (the whiskers). For groups, `ax.boxplot()` takes a **list**, one
Series per box, and `ax.set_xticks()` names the boxes.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Box plots of adult asthma prevalence for metro and nonmetro Pennsylvania counties. The boxes overlap heavily; the nonmetro median is 10.7 percent and the metro median is 10.5 percent."
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "metro"]],       # attach metro status ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

levels = ["Metro", "Nonmetro"]                             # the groups, in display order
groups = [joined.loc[joined["metro"] == m,                 # rows in group m ...
                     "asthma_prev_pct"]                    # ... asthma column only
          for m in levels]                                 # one Series per group

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.boxplot(groups)                                         # one box per Series in the list
ax.set_xticks([1, 2], levels)                              # boxes sit at x = 1, 2: name them
ax.set_ylabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title("Asthma by metro status")                     # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 3.** Box plots of adult asthma prevalence for metro and nonmetro Pennsylvania counties. The boxes overlap heavily; the nonmetro median is 10.7 percent and the metro median is 10.5 percent.
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex3_boxplot
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # region per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "region"]],      # attach region ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

regions = sorted(joined["region"].unique())                # the six regions, alphabetical
groups = [joined.loc[joined["region"] == r,                # rows in region r ...
                     "smoking_prev_pct"]                   # ... smoking column only
          for r in regions]                                # one Series per region

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))                   # canvas and one axes
ax.boxplot(groups)                                         # one box per Series
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 7), regions, rotation=30)           # name the six boxes
ax.set_title("Adult smoking by region")                    # figure title
ax.set_ylabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)",              # y-axis label with units
              fontsize=13)                                 # larger than the default 10
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

```{pyodide}

assert sum(len(g) for g in groups) == 67, "Every county belongs to exactly one box."   # nothing lost
```

# Exercise 4 — Scatter shows co-movement {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 4 — Scatter shows co-movement {.smaller}

**Worked example.** `ax.scatter()` places one point per row, using two columns as coordinates.
It is the figure to draw before trusting any correlation.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of adult asthma prevalence against adult smoking prevalence across 67 Pennsylvania counties, rising from left to right with a correlation of 0.659."
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
r = asthma["smoking_prev_pct"].corr(asthma["asthma_prev_pct"])   # co-movement, -1 to +1

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))                   # canvas and one axes
ax.scatter(asthma["smoking_prev_pct"],                     # x: smoking
           asthma["asthma_prev_pct"],                      # y: asthma
           color="#003594", s=40, alpha=0.8,               # colour, size, transparency
           edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)               # white rim around each point
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")              # x-axis label with units
ax.set_ylabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title(f"Asthma against smoking, 67 counties (r = {r:.3f})")  # the finding in the title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 4.** Scatter plot of adult asthma prevalence against adult smoking prevalence across 67 Pennsylvania counties, rising from left to right with a correlation of 0.659.
:::

## Exercise 4 — Scatter shows co-movement — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Draw infant mortality against **child poverty** for the reporting counties, and
put the correlation in the title. Child poverty is `children_in_poverty_pct`, on the x-axis; `r` is its correlation with `infant_mortality_per_1000`, using the same `reporting` rows as Exercise 1.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
import pandas as pd                                        # tables

births = pd.read_csv("data/pa_maternal_infant.csv")        # one row per county
reporting = births.dropna(subset=["infant_mortality_per_1000"])  # drop suppressed counties

r = reporting["children_in_poverty_pct"].____(reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"])  # co-movement

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))                   # canvas and one axes
ax.scatter(reporting["children_in_poverty_pct"],           # x: child poverty
           reporting["infant_mortality_per_1000"],         # y: infant mortality

           edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)               # white rim around each point

ax.set_ylabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")       # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality against child poverty, 44 counties (r = {r:.3f})")  # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

print("r =", round(r, 3))                                  # the correlation
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
#| hint: true
# The blank is corr.
#
# series_a.corr(series_b) returns a single number between -1 and +1.
```

```{pyodide}
ax.set_xlabel("Children in poverty (%)")                   # x-axis label with units
ax.set_ylabel("Infant deaths per 1,000 live births")       # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title(f"Infant mortality against child poverty, 44 counties (r = {r:.3f})")  # title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

print("r =", round(r, 3))                                  # the correlation
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex4_scatter
#| check: true
assert abs(r - 0.6465) < 0.01, "Child poverty and infant mortality correlate at +0.646."  # right r
assert len(ax.collections) >= 1, "ax.scatter must draw the points."                    # points drawn
assert "0.6" in ax.get_title(), "Put the correlation in the title."                    # r in title
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## This is a statement about counties
Counties with more children in poverty bury more infants. The mechanism is structural —
prenatal care access, distance to obstetric services, housing, and food security. The figure
describes counties, never individual families.
:::

# Exercise 5 — Mapping versus setting {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 5 — Mapping versus setting {.smaller}

**Worked example.** seaborn takes a DataFrame and **column names**. A keyword that names a
column is a **mapping**: `hue=` drives colour from the data, and seaborn builds the legend. A
keyword that takes a constant, such as `color=` or `marker=`, is a **setting**.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Seaborn scatter plot of adult asthma against adult smoking for 67 Pennsylvania counties, coloured by metro status in royal blue and dark gold, with a legend titled Metro status."
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "metro"]],       # attach metro status ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))                   # canvas and one axes
sns.scatterplot(data=joined,                               # data
                x="smoking_prev_pct",                      # MAPPING: smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # MAPPING: asthma -> y
                hue="metro",                               # MAPPING: metro -> colour
                palette={"Metro": "#003594",               # colours for the hue groups
                         "Nonmetro": "#8a6400"},           # dark gold for nonmetro
                s=50,                                      # SETTING: one size for every point
                ax=ax)                                     # draw on this axes
ax.set(xlabel="Adult smoking prevalence (%)",              # x-axis label with units
       ylabel="Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # y-axis label with units
ax.get_legend().set_title("Metro status")                  # replace the column-name title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 5.** Seaborn scatter plot of adult asthma against adult smoking for 67 Pennsylvania counties, coloured by metro status in royal blue and dark gold, with a legend titled Metro status.
:::

# Exercise 6 — Two series need two channels {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 6 — Two series need two channels {.smaller}

**Worked example.** Royal and dark gold each pass contrast against the page, but separate from
each other by only 2.02:1. A second channel — here a marker shape plus a legend — is what makes
the groups distinguishable.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of adult obesity against adult smoking prevalence for 67 Pennsylvania counties, with metro counties drawn as circles and nonmetro counties as triangles, plus a legend."
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "metro"]],       # attach metro status ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))                   # canvas and one axes
for group, colour, marker in [("Metro", "#003594", "o"),   # one layer per group, with its
                              ("Nonmetro", "#8a6400", "^")]:  # own colour AND its own shape
    subset = joined[joined["metro"] == group]              # counties in this group
    ax.scatter(subset["smoking_prev_pct"],                 # x: smoking
               subset["obesity_prev_pct"],                 # y: obesity
               color=colour, marker=marker, s=42,          # colour, shape, size
               label=group)                                # legend entry for this layer
ax.set_xlabel("Adult smoking prevalence (%)")              # x-axis label with units
ax.set_ylabel("Adult obesity prevalence (%)")              # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title("Obesity against smoking, by metro status")   # title
ax.legend(frameon=False)                                   # legend from each layer's label=
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 6.** Scatter plot of adult obesity against adult smoking prevalence for 67 Pennsylvania counties, with metro counties drawn as circles and nonmetro counties as triangles, plus a legend.
:::

# Exercise 7 — A line needs an ordered axis {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 7 — A line needs an ordered axis {.smaller}

**Worked example.** A line asserts that consecutive points are connected, which is meaningful
only when the x-axis has an order, such as time. `sns.lineplot()` maps `style=` to the **dash
pattern**, so each line differs by more than colour. The COVID file is filtered to **August 2021
onward**: it badly undercounts 2020, and a figure drawn from those months would be false.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Seaborn line chart of monthly COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 residents in Allegheny and Philadelphia counties from August 2021 to March 2024. Allegheny is solid and Philadelphia dashed; both peak in January 2022, Philadelphia at 35.9 and Allegheny at 26.3, then fall close to zero."
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")           # deaths by county and month
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # population per county
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])            # text -> real dates
covid = covid[covid["month"] >= "2021-08-01"]              # keep the reliably reported period

two = covid[covid["county"].isin(["Allegheny", "Philadelphia"])]   # the two largest counties
two = two.merge(counties[["county", "population_2023"]],   # attach each county's population
                on="county")                               # ... matched by county name
two["per_100k"] = (two["covid_deaths"]                     # deaths ...
                   / two["population_2023"] * 100000)      # ... per 100,000 residents

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
sns.lineplot(data=two, x="month", y="per_100k",            # data; time -> x, rate -> y
             hue="county", style="county",                 # county -> colour AND dash pattern
             palette={"Allegheny": "#003594",              # course colours, by name
                      "Philadelphia": "#8a6400"},          # dark gold for Philadelphia
             linewidth=2, ax=ax)                           # SETTING: line width; target axes
ax.set(xlabel="Month",                                     # x-axis label
       ylabel="COVID-19 deaths per 100,000")               # y-axis label with units
ax.get_legend().set_title("County")                        # legend title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 7.** Seaborn line chart of monthly COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 residents in Allegheny and Philadelphia counties from August 2021 to March 2024. Allegheny is solid and Philadelphia dashed; both peak in January 2022, Philadelphia at 35.9 and Allegheny at 26.3, then fall close to zero.
:::

## Exercise 7 — A line needs an ordered axis — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Compare **metro and nonmetro** Pennsylvania. Total the deaths and the population
of each group for each month, compute deaths per 100,000, and draw one line per group with
`sns.lineplot()`, mapping `metro` to both colour and dash pattern. Use the rows from August
2021 onward. `monthly` has one row per month and metro group, with columns `month`, `metro`,
`covid_deaths`, `population_2023`, and `per_100k`.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_line
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")           # deaths by county and month
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # population and metro per county
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])            # text -> real dates
covid = covid[covid["month"] >= "2021-08-01"]              # keep the reliably reported period

merged = covid.merge(counties[["county", "population_2023", "metro"]],  # attach population
                     on="county")                                       # and metro status
monthly = (merged.____(["month", "metro"], as_index=False)              # one row per month x group
                 [["covid_deaths", "population_2023"]].sum())           # total deaths and people
monthly["per_100k"] = (monthly["covid_deaths"]             # deaths ...
                       / monthly["population_2023"]        # ... per resident ...
                       * 100000)                           # ... per 100,000

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
sns.lineplot(data=monthly, x="month", y="per_100k",        # data; time -> x, rate -> y
             hue="metro", ____="metro",                    # metro -> colour AND dash pattern
             palette={"Metro": "#003594",                  # course colours, by group
                      "Nonmetro": "#8a6400"},              # dark gold for nonmetro
             linewidth=2, ax=ax)                           # SETTING: line width; target axes
ax.set(xlabel="Month",                                     # x-axis label
       ylabel="COVID-19 deaths per 100,000")               # y-axis label with units
ax.get_legend().set_title("Metro status")                  # legend title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

peaks = monthly.loc[monthly.groupby("metro")["per_100k"].idxmax()]   # each group's worst month
print(peaks[["metro", "month", "per_100k"]].round(1).to_string(index=False))  # print the peaks
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_line
#| hint: true
# The first blank is groupby; the second is style.
#
# Summing population_2023 within a month and group gives that group's
# total population, because each county appears once per month. That is
# what makes per_100k a rate for the whole group.
#
# Nonmetro counties peak first and higher: 44.2 per 100,000 in December
# 2021, against 32.9 for metro counties in January 2022.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_line
#| solution: true
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")           # deaths by county and month
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # population and metro per county
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])            # text -> real dates
covid = covid[covid["month"] >= "2021-08-01"]              # keep the reliably reported period

merged = covid.merge(counties[["county", "population_2023", "metro"]],  # attach population
                     on="county")                                       # and metro status
monthly = (merged.groupby(["month", "metro"], as_index=False)           # one row per month x group
                 [["covid_deaths", "population_2023"]].sum())           # total deaths and people
monthly["per_100k"] = (monthly["covid_deaths"]             # deaths ...
                       / monthly["population_2023"]        # ... per resident ...
                       * 100000)                           # ... per 100,000

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
sns.lineplot(data=monthly, x="month", y="per_100k",        # data; time -> x, rate -> y
             hue="metro", style="metro",                   # metro -> colour AND dash pattern
             palette={"Metro": "#003594",                  # course colours, by group
                      "Nonmetro": "#8a6400"},              # dark gold for nonmetro
             linewidth=2, ax=ax)                           # SETTING: line width; target axes
ax.set(xlabel="Month",                                     # x-axis label
       ylabel="COVID-19 deaths per 100,000")               # y-axis label with units
ax.get_legend().set_title("Metro status")                  # legend title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

peaks = monthly.loc[monthly.groupby("metro")["per_100k"].idxmax()]   # each group's worst month
print(peaks[["metro", "month", "per_100k"]].round(1).to_string(index=False))  # print the peaks
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex7_line
#| check: true
assert len(monthly) == 64, "32 months from August 2021, times two groups."            # right rows
assert monthly["month"].min() == pd.Timestamp("2021-08-01"), "Start at August 2021."  # filter applied
nonmetro = monthly[monthly["metro"] == "Nonmetro"]                                    # one group's rows
assert abs(nonmetro["per_100k"].max() - 44.2) < 0.1, "Nonmetro peaks at 44.2 per 100,000."  # it is a rate
assert len({l.get_linestyle() for l in ax.lines}) >= 2, "Map style= so the lines differ by dash pattern."  # 2nd channel
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rates compare places of different size
Nonmetro Pennsylvania peaked first and higher, per resident. A chart of death **counts** would
show the reverse, because metro counties hold most of the population. Module 6 makes that
difference its centrepiece.
:::

# Exercise 8 — Repair a truncated axis {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Exercise 8 — Repair a truncated axis {.smaller}

**This figure runs without error and it is misleading.** A bar encodes value by length, so its
baseline must be zero. `set_ylim(10.2, 10.9)` breaks the correspondence between length and value.

```{pyodide}
#| fig-alt: "Misleading bar chart of mean adult asthma prevalence for six Pennsylvania regions with the y-axis truncated to the range 10.2 to 10.9 percent, which makes a 0.36 point spread look like a large difference."
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # region per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "region"]],      # attach region ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

by_region = (joined.groupby("region")["asthma_prev_pct"]   # one mean per region ...
                   .mean().sort_values())                  # ... in ascending order

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.bar(by_region.index, by_region.values, color="#003594") # one bar per region
ax.set_ylim(10.2, 10.9)                                    # <- the distortion
ax.set_ylabel("Mean adult asthma (%)")                     # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title("MISLEADING: regional asthma differences look large")  # title
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=7)    # tilt and shrink region names
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 8.** Misleading bar chart of mean adult asthma prevalence for six Pennsylvania regions with the y-axis truncated to the range 10.2 to 10.9 percent, which makes a 0.36 point spread look like a large difference.
:::

## Exercise 8 — Repair a truncated axis — your turn {.smaller}

**Your turn.** Repair it. Set the lower limit to zero so the bar lengths match the values. Set the limits to `(0, 12)`, and replace the `MISLEADING` title with one that describes the chart. `spread` is the highest regional mean minus the lowest.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_truncated
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # region per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "region"]],      # attach region ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

by_region = (joined.groupby("region")["asthma_prev_pct"]   # one mean per region ...
                   .mean().sort_values())                  # ... in ascending order

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.bar(by_region.index, by_region.values, color="#003594") # one bar per region
ax.set_ylim(____, 12)                                      # the baseline a bar requires
ax.set_ylabel("Mean adult asthma (%)")                     # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title("Mean county asthma prevalence by region")    # a title that describes the chart
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=7)    # tilt and shrink region names
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

spread = by_region.max() - by_region.min()                 # highest mean minus lowest
print("baseline:", ax.get_ylim()[0])                       # the repaired lower limit
print("true spread across six regions:", round(spread, 2), "percentage points")  # the real gap
```

```{pyodide}
# Compare the two figures. The truncated version implies the North Central
# region has a dramatically higher asthma burden than the Southeast. The
# real difference is 0.36 percentage points across all six regions.
# Nobody has to intend this: a plotting library that auto-scales to the
# data range produces the top panel by default.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_truncated
#| solution: true
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # region per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties[["county", "region"]],      # attach region ...
                      on="county", how="left")             # ... keeping every county

by_region = (joined.groupby("region")["asthma_prev_pct"]   # one mean per region ...
                   .mean().sort_values())                  # ... in ascending order

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))                     # canvas and one axes
ax.bar(by_region.index, by_region.values, color="#003594") # one bar per region
ax.set_ylim(0, 12)                                         # the baseline a bar requires
ax.set_ylabel("Mean adult asthma (%)")                     # y-axis label with units
ax.set_title("Mean county asthma prevalence by region")    # a title that describes the chart
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=7)    # tilt and shrink region names
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure

spread = by_region.max() - by_region.min()                 # highest mean minus lowest
print("baseline:", ax.get_ylim()[0])                       # the repaired lower limit
print("true spread across six regions:", round(spread, 2), "percentage points")  # the real gap
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex8_truncated
#| check: true
assert ax.get_ylim()[0] == 0, "A bar chart's baseline must be zero."                   # repaired
assert abs(spread - 0.36) < 0.01, "The true spread across six regions is 0.36 points." # the real gap
assert len(ax.patches) == 6, "Six regions, six bars."                                  # six bars
```

# Done {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## What this lab covered {.smaller}

- `ax.hist()` with a reference line from `ax.axvline()`, and the counties a figure leaves out
- `ax.barh()` with sorted bars; **zero baselines** for every bar chart
- `ax.boxplot()` for groups: one Series per box, named with `ax.set_xticks()`
- `ax.scatter()` and `.corr()` as co-movement between counties, never as cause
- seaborn: **mapping** a column with `hue=` against **setting** a constant with `marker=`
- A **second channel** for every grouping: marker shape, dash pattern, legend
- `sns.lineplot()` over an ordered time axis, with **rates** rather than counts

::: {.callout-tip}

Exercise 8 executed cleanly and made six regions look far apart, when their means span only
0.36 percentage points. **Running is not checking.**
:::
